def norm_text(s):
    """Collapse hard line wraps inside paragraphs; keep blank-line paragraph breaks."""
    s = re.sub(r"(?<=[A-Za-z0-9])-[ \t]*\n\s*(?=[a-z])", "-", s)  # compound split at a hard wrap
    paras = re.split(r"\n\s*\n", s.strip())

SPEAKER = r"(?:(?:Mr|Ms|Mrs|Dr)\. )?[A-Z][A-Za-z]+(?: [A-Za-z]+)?: "


def speaker_breaks(s):
    """In a dialogue stimulus, start each later speaker on its own line (matches the database convention)."""
    if not re.match(SPEAKER, s):

    def brk(m):

    return re.sub(r"(\S*[.?!”\"])\s+(?=" + SPEAKER + ")", brk, s)

## PT156-S2-Q17 | Must Be True | D

> To measure a small boat hull accurately, it is necessary to level the hull so that a baseline can be established. This does not require sophisticated tools, but it does require a leveling tool called a “line level.” When scientists discovered a small ninth-century boat, they wanted to record the dimensions of its hull accurately. None of the scientists, however, had any experience measuring hulls. Because of this they were not sure they had leveled the hull before establishing a baseline.
>
> If the statements above are true, then which one of the following must also be true?
>
> (A) The scientists did not accurately measure the hull’s dimensions because they had no experience measuring hulls.
> (B) The scientists accurately determined the hull’s dimensions, provided that they leveled the hull.
> (C) If the scientists did not accurately determine the hull’s dimensions, it was because they did not have a line level.
> (D) The scientists were able to accurately record the hull’s dimensions only if they used a line level.
> (E) If the scientists had measured the hull’s dimensions accurately, then at least one of them would have had experience measuring hulls.

### Argument Breakdown

**Statements:** Accurately measuring a hull requires leveling it. Leveling requires a line level. The scientists weren't sure they had leveled the hull.

**Evaluate:** Chain the requirements: accurate measurement → leveled → used a line level. So an accurate measurement requires a line level. Notice what we *don't* know: whether they leveled it or measured accurately.

**Goal:** They measured accurately only if they used a line level.

### Choice Notes

**(A) Unsupported.** They weren't *sure* they leveled it. They might have. We can't conclude the measurement was wrong.

**(B) Reversed.** Leveling is required for accuracy, not enough for it. They could level the hull and still measure badly.

**(C) Unsupported.** A missing line level is one way to fail, not the only one. They could have had one and still erred.

**(D) Correct.** Accurate → leveled → line level. "Only if" states the requirement.

**(E) Unsupported.** Experience is never said to be required. Inexperienced people could get lucky and level it correctly.

184	  D All organisms with large brains are biologically equipped for flexible behavior.
185	  E Only organisms with brains of insect size or smaller engage in purely instinctual behavior.

191	  STEP Facts | conditionals (must, no, universal noun)
192	Flexible —requires→ large # of neurons behavior
193	Insect brain → doesn't have large # of neurons Instinctual → No reasoning and behavior fewer nerve cells than flex behavior
194	  STEP Evaluate | The #1 thing we read for on MBT is conditionals. We found three of them. Do they chain together? Do they have any overlapping concepts?
195	Yes, two of them mention flexible behavior. Two of them mention a large # of neurons. The last two claims chain together to give us this,
196	Insect → not large # → not flexible brain of neurons behavior
197	That idea of "not flexible" behavior is the same as instinctual behavior, so we could also chain on the first claim.
198	Insect → not large # → not flexible → no reasoning brain of neurons behavior fewer nerve cells
199	  STEP Goal | Let's look for anything we can prove. It'll probably reward us for having assembled this chain, though not necessarily with a Head → Tail inference.
200	  STEP Conclusion | Fact-set, no conclusion offered.
201	  STEP Evidence | Flexible behavior needs many neurons. Insect brains don't have enough.
202	  STEP Evaluate | Insects can't produce flexible behavior, so all their behavior is instinctual.
203	  STEP Goal | Find the answer about insect behavior being exclusively instinctual.
204	  STEP Conclusion | This is a fact-set, not an argument. Your job is to chain the facts and find what they force.
205	  STEP Evidence | The setup is a clean conditional chain. Flexible behavior requires a brain with many neurons. Insect brains do not have many neurons (at least not enough). Behavior is split into two types — instinctual or flexible.
206	  STEP Evaluate | Walk the chain. Insects don't have enough neurons → insects can't produce flexible behavior → if insect behavior exists, it must be the other kind, instinctual.
207	So everything insects do, behavior-wise, is instinctual. That's the modest, direct conclusion the facts force.
208	Watch out for trap answers that try to extend the inference to all organisms, to non-insects, to brain-elaborate organisms in general — the passage only gives us facts about insects specifically.
209	  STEP Goal | Pick the answer that says insect behavior is exclusively instinctual.
210	  NOTE A | This claims that elaborate-brain organisms *usually* behave non-instinctually. The passage tells us they have the capacity for flexible behavior, but it never says how often they use it. They could spend most of their time on instinct and only occasionally use flexibility. The "usually" is unsupported.
211	  NOTE B | This is exactly the inference the chain forces. The passage gives a clean two-option dichotomy: behavior is instinctual or flexible (noninstinctual). Flexible behavior needs many neurons. Insect brains don't have many.
212	
213	So insects can't do flexible behavior. The only kind they can do is instinctual. That makes their behavior exclusively instinctual — which is exactly what (B) says.
214	  NOTE C | The passage tells us insect brains fall below the neuron threshold for flexible behavior. It says nothing about whether *every* non-insect organism clears that threshold. Plenty of small animals might still have brains too small for flexibility. "All organisms with brains larger than insects'" is much too sweeping.
215	  NOTE D | The passage requires "a large number of neurons" for flexible behavior. This answer talks about "large brains," which isn't quite the same — different organisms pack neurons differently, and not every large-brained organism has the right kind of neuron density. The passage also doesn't commit to "all" large-brained organisms being capable.
216	  NOTE E | This answer says only insect-or-smaller-brained organisms do purely instinctual behavior. The passage tells us insects fall below the neuron threshold, so they're instinct-only. But it doesn't say no other animal does. There could be non-insect animals also limited to instinct. The "only" is too strong.

511	  STEP Evaluate | Barr is leaning entirely on the Survey Group's sales numbers. The whole argument rises or falls on whether those numbers really tell us about tea drinking nationwide.

Sixteen are in the database with no explanation, one needs steps only, and twelve are not in the database.\n\nSix unloaded slots are filed as Must Be True but ask something else, and load with the correct type:\n- Sufficient Assumption: PT144-S4-Q1, PT145-S4-Q24, PT156-S2-Q18, PT156-S2-Q25, PT156-S4-Q22.\n- Flaw: PT156-S4-Q23.\n\nModelled on `models/MBT-MBF.md`: chain the conditionals, name what the facts force, and kill wrong answers as Unsupported, Reversed, Too Strong, or Opposite.\n\nLabels: Must Be True: Statements / Evaluate / Goal. Sufficient Assumption and Flaw: Conclusion / Evidence / Evaluate / Goal.\n\n## PT101-S3-Q15 | Must Be True | E\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Many of Dr. Q's characterizations of Dr. Z's work are imprecise. Such imprecise characterizations do not give an adequate basis for sound criticism.\n\n**Evaluate:** \"Such characterizations\" points back to the imprecise ones. So: many characterizations are imprecise, and every imprecise one fails as a basis for criticism. \"Many\" guarantees at least one. So at least one characterization fails as a basis for criticism. We learn nothing about the precise ones.\n\n**Goal:** At least one of Dr. Q's characterizations fails to give an adequate basis for criticism.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Unsupported.** We know nothing about the precise characterizations. Every one of Dr. Q's characterizations could be imprecise, and then none would work.\n\n**(B) Unsupported.** This assumes precision is enough for a sound basis. Dr. Z only says imprecision is enough to fail.\n\n**(C) Reversed.** Dr. Z says imprecise → inadequate. This says inadequate → imprecise. A characterization could be precise and still inadequate for some other reason.\n\n**(D) Unsupported.** Same mistake as (B), now stated as a general rule about anyone's work.\n\n**(E) Correct.** Many characterizations are imprecise, and imprecise ones are inadequate. So at least one is inadequate.\n\n## PT103-S2-Q6 | Must Be True | D\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** The largest volcano on Mars is enormous. No volcano that size could exist on Earth, even with Mars's low gravity, because Earth's crust is too thin to hold that mass.\n\n**Evaluate:** Gravity is set aside on purpose (\"even if\"), and the crusts are the same material. The only difference left is thickness. Mars's crust does hold the volcano, so at least where the volcano sits, Mars's crust must be thicker than Earth's.\n\n**Goal:** Mars's crust is thicker than Earth's at some point.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Unsupported.** Erosion never comes up.\n\n**(B) Too Strong.** We know the crust under this one volcano is thick enough. We know nothing about where the other high volcanoes sit or where the crust is thickest.\n\n**(C) Unsupported.** We know about the largest volcano on each planet, not the average height of volcanoes.\n\n**(D) Correct.** Same material, gravity set aside, and Mars holds a mass Earth's crust could not. Mars's crust must be thicker at least there.\n\n**(E) Unsupported.** A thicker crust would let Earth support bigger volcanoes. That doesn't mean any real volcano would actually be bigger. Volcanoes need magma and eruptions too.\n\n## PT103-S3-Q7 | Must Be True | E\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Lack of exercise causes effects like aging. Appropriate exercise can often slow the changes of aging. No drug holds any promise of slowing them.\n\n**Evaluate:** The blank follows \"Therefore,\" so it has to be what the facts support. Exercise often works. Drugs hold no promise. So if you want to slow aging, exercise is the better bet.\n\n**Goal:** To slow aging, exercise is more practical than drugs.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Unsupported.** Drugs have no promise of slowing aging. That doesn't mean they speed it up the way lack of exercise does.\n\n**(B) Unsupported.** Nothing says people who skip exercise need drugs. Drugs are actually described as useless for aging.\n\n**(C) Too Strong.** Exercise can often slow the changes. Prevent is much stronger than slow.\n\n**(D) Unsupported.** Age at which exercise starts never comes up.\n\n**(E) Correct.** Exercise often slows aging. Drugs hold no promise. Exercise is the more practical choice.\n\n## PT104-S4-Q17 | Must Be True | A\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** If any corporate sponsor had withdrawn support, the Green Ensemble would have been forced to disband this year. The group did not disband. It kept running and announced next year's schedule.\n\n**Evaluate:** Sponsor withdrew → disband. The group didn't disband. Take the contrapositive: no sponsor withdrew.\n\n**Goal:** No corporate sponsor withdrew support this year.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** Withdrawal would have forced the group to disband. It didn't disband, so no sponsor withdrew.\n\n**(B) Unsupported.** The group has \"always been\" dependent on corporations. Nothing says it found other money.\n\n**(C) Unsupported.** We know funding didn't fall away. We don't know it rose.\n\n**(D) Unsupported.** Dependence doesn't tell us what share of income came from corporations.\n\n**(E) Unsupported.** The passage is about one group, not funding for theater groups in general.\n\n## PT105-S2-Q7 | Must Be True | E\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Creativity is, at its core, the ability to make variations on a theme. Every scientific idea is built on many related ideas. Every new theme or discovery is always, without exception, a variation on earlier themes.\n\n**Evaluate:** This is an EXCEPT question, so four answers follow from the passage and one does not. Look for the answer that breaks \"always and without exception.\" Any answer saying some discovery is not a variation contradicts the passage.\n\n**Goal:** Find the answer that says some discovery is not a variation on earlier themes.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Must be true.** If creativity is the ability to make variations, lacking that ability means lacking creativity.\n\n**(B) Must be true.** Every idea is built on a thousand related ideas, so none is fully independent.\n\n**(C) Must be true.** Careful analysis shows every discovery is a variation of earlier themes, so analysis can reveal those themes.\n\n**(D) Must be true.** Every discovery is a variation on a theme. Anyone who made a great discovery made such a variation.\n\n**(E) Correct.** The passage says every discovery is a variation, \"always and without exception.\" This says some are not. It contradicts the passage.\n\n## PT106-S1-Q14 | Must Be True | B\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Earth's tilt can stay stable only because of the Moon's gravity. Without a stable, moderate tilt, a planet's climate can't support life. Mars has small moons, a wild tilt, and no life.\n\n**Evaluate:** Chain the requirements. Support life → stable tilt. For Earth, stable tilt → the Moon. So Earth supporting life → the Moon. Take the contrapositive: no Moon → no stable tilt → no life.\n\n**Goal:** If Earth lost its Moon, Earth's climate couldn't support life.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Reversed.** A large moon is required for a stable tilt, and a stable tilt is required for life. Neither is enough. Mars might still fail for other reasons.\n\n**(B) Correct.** Without the Moon, Earth's tilt can't stay stable, and without a stable tilt, the climate can't support life.\n\n**(C) Reversed.** A stable tilt is required for life, not enough for it.\n\n**(D) Unsupported.** The passage names the Moon as the stabilizer. It never says other forces have little effect on the tilt.\n\n**(E) Unsupported.** The number of moons never matters. Size and closeness do.\n\n## PT113-S2-Q12 | Must Be True | A\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Good meal → good food. Good food → good soil. Good soil → good farming. Good farming → a culture that values maintaining natural resources.\n\n**Evaluate:** Rosen gives a chain of requirements. Link it: good meal → good food → good soil → good farming → the right culture. So a good meal requires good soil, which is a natural condition, and the right culture, which is a cultural condition.\n\n**Goal:** Good meals depend on both natural and cultural conditions.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** Follow the chain. Good meals need good soil (natural) and, further down, a culture that values resources (cultural).\n\n**(B) Reversed.** Rosen says good farming requires the right culture. Nothing says maintaining natural resources requires good farming.\n\n**(C) Reversed.** Good soil requires good farming. This says good farming requires good soil.\n\n**(D) Reversed.** Good culture is required for good meals, not enough for them.\n\n**(E) Reversed.** Bad food isn't traced back to a single cause. Good soil is required for good food, but food can go bad in other ways.\n\n## PT113-S3-Q17 | Must Be True | A\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Purists want to ban nonaddictive drugs before competition because they are unnatural. The author answers that almost everything in sports is unnatural, from running shoes to gloves to machines, and none of it is banned for being unnatural. The author concludes that nonaddictive drugs should not be banned.\n\n**Evaluate:** The author rejects the purists' reason as \"ridiculous\" because being unnatural has never been grounds for a ban. So the author treats unnaturalness alone as not enough to justify banning something.\n\n**Goal:** Being unnatural is not, by itself, a good enough reason to ban something.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** The author's rebuttal only works if being unnatural is not enough to justify a ban.\n\n**(B) Opposite.** The author concedes that almost everything in sports is unnatural, and never denies that drugs are.\n\n**(C) Unsupported.** Addictive drugs are unjustified because they are physically harmful, not because they are unnatural.\n\n**(D) Unsupported.** The author says serious problems cause deaths and injuries, but never says addictive drugs are among them.\n\n**(E) Unsupported.** The passage never compares addictive drugs with injuries.\n\n## PT115-S4-Q10 | Must Be True | B\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Profit per bottle equals wholesale price minus production costs. The wholesale price is the same as in 1991. Every cost is the same except corks, which nearly doubled.\n\n**Evaluate:** Price stays flat, total cost rises because of the corks. Price minus a bigger cost is a smaller number. So each bottle earns less profit now. This is about one bottle, not total sales.\n\n**Goal:** Each bottle sold today earns less profit than each bottle sold in 1991.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Unsupported.** Sales volume never comes up.\n\n**(B) Correct.** Same price minus a higher cost leaves less profit per bottle.\n\n**(C) Unsupported.** The winegrower pays more for corks. That could be the cork maker raising prices, not its own costs rising.\n\n**(D) Unsupported.** Total profit depends on how many bottles were sold. If sales grew enough, total profit could be higher even with thinner margins.\n\n**(E) Unsupported.** Corks doubled in price, but we don't know how they compare with the bottles. A cork could still cost far less than a bottle.\n\n## PT116-S2-Q22 | Must Be True | A\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** All parrots can learn to speak a few words. Some parrots native to Australia can be counted on for a sweet temper. Almost any hand-fed parrot shows great affection for its owner.\n\n**Evaluate:** Combine the \"all\" with the \"some.\" Every parrot can learn to speak. Some parrots (some Australian ones) are sweet tempered. So some parrots that can learn to speak are sweet tempered.\n\n**Goal:** Some speaking-capable parrots are sweet tempered.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** All parrots can learn to speak, and some are sweet tempered, so some sweet-tempered parrots can learn to speak.\n\n**(B) Unsupported.** Hand-feeding produces affection for the owner. Nothing says it's the only way a non-Australian parrot can be sweet tempered.\n\n**(C) Unsupported.** Some Australian parrots are reliably sweet. That doesn't make them the sweetest.\n\n**(D) Unsupported.** Parrots from other places could also be sweet tempered. The passage only mentions Australia.\n\n**(E) Too Strong.** Only some Australian parrots are counted on for a sweet temper. This says all Australian pet birds.\n\n## PT116-S3-Q24 | Must Be True | B\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Some recent graduates care about work environment. All recent graduates care about salary and vacation policy. The only workers who care about stress level are a few veteran employees.\n\n**Evaluate:** Connect the \"some\" to the \"all.\" Some recent graduates care about work environment, and every recent graduate cares about vacation policy. So those graduates care about both. That gives us at least some people who care about work environment and vacation policy.\n\n**Goal:** Some people who care about work environment also care about vacation policy.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Too Strong.** We only know about recent graduates. Other people could care about work environment and not salary.\n\n**(B) Correct.** The graduates who care about work environment also care about vacation policy, since every graduate does.\n\n**(C) Unsupported.** The passage says nothing about how veteran employees view work environment.\n\n**(D) Reversed.** All graduates care about vacation and salary, but other people who care about vacation policy might not care about salary.\n\n**(E) Unsupported.** The veterans who care about stress level could also care about salary. Nothing rules that out.\n\n## PT117-S3-Q7 | Must Be True | C\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** No keyboarding skills → can't use a computer. Can't use a computer → can't write essays in a word processor.\n\n**Evaluate:** Chain them: no keyboarding → no computer → no word processing. The contrapositive runs backward: word processing → computer → some keyboarding skills.\n\n**Goal:** If you can write essays in a word processor, you have some keyboarding skills.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Negated.** Having some skill avoids the trigger, but that doesn't guarantee success. You might still fail for other reasons.\n\n**(B) Reversed.** This runs the chain backward. You could have keyboarding skills and fail to write essays for another reason.\n\n**(C) Correct.** This is the contrapositive of the chain. Word processing → computer → keyboarding.\n\n**(D) Unsupported.** Using a computer is required for word processing, not enough for it. \"Probably\" isn't supported either.\n\n**(E) Reversed.** This flips the second statement. Failing to word-process doesn't prove you can't use a computer.\n\n## PT118-S3-Q14 | Must Be True | E\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** In theory, analog beats digital because analog signals can be infinitely detailed. In practice, copying an analog signal introduces tiny errors. The errors pile up with each copy until noise wipes out the original information.\n\n**Evaluate:** The pivot \"however\" brings in the practical problem, and it is specific: duplication. Each copy adds errors. So when a signal must be copied many times, analog breaks down, and digital, which lacks unlimited detail, comes out ahead.\n\n**Goal:** Digital beats analog when a signal must be reproduced many times.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Too Strong.** One example of theory failing in practice says nothing about many ideas.\n\n**(B) Unsupported.** The problem is error buildup from copying, not that we don't need infinite detail.\n\n**(C) Too Strong.** We're never told digital signals are error-free, and \"the best\" is far beyond the passage.\n\n**(D) Too Strong.** Analog only fails with repeated copying. We don't know that's true for most practical purposes.\n\n**(E) Correct.** Analog's weakness is duplication. When signals are copied many times, digital wins.\n\n## PT119-S2-Q7 | Must Be True | B\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Behavior is either instinctual or flexible. Flexible behavior requires a brain with a large number of neurons. No insect brain has enough neurons.\n\n**Evaluate:** Chain it. Insect brain → not enough neurons → no flexible behavior. Behavior that isn't flexible is instinctual. So everything insects do is instinctual.\n\n**Goal:** Insect behavior is entirely instinctual.\n\n## PT119-S3-Q11 | Must Be True | B\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Queenston added 30 percent more teachers between 1990 and 1993. The average number of students per teacher didn't change.\n\n**Evaluate:** Students per teacher is students divided by teachers. If teachers went up 30 percent and the ratio stayed flat, students must also have gone up, by 30 percent.\n\n**Goal:** Total enrollment increased.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Unsupported.** The average is flat, but individual classes could have grown while others shrank.\n\n**(B) Correct.** More teachers with the same ratio means more students.\n\n**(C) Unsupported.** The budget got larger. We don't know by how much, and teachers aren't the only cost.\n\n**(D) Unsupported.** Teacher turnover never comes up. The count grew, but the people could have changed.\n\n**(E) Unsupported.** Quality of education never comes up, and the student-teacher ratio didn't even improve.\n\n## PT121-S4-Q14 | Must Be True | D\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** The tax law aims to increase forested land by rewarding companies for reforesting cleared land. One company bought and reforested a cleared tract to cut its taxes. It paid for this by clearing a larger tract it had planned to keep in reserve.\n\n**Evaluate:** The company collected the incentive, but cleared more land than it replanted. The law's goal is more forest. The company's actions produced less. So the law can push a company to act against the law's purpose while still getting the tax break.\n\n**Goal:** The law can motivate behavior that works against its own purpose.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Too Strong.** One company's case doesn't show the law fails across the region. The company did reforest a tract.\n\n**(B) Opposite.** The law already had an effect: one tract replanted and a larger one cleared.\n\n**(C) Unsupported.** We have no basis to predict how much land companies will eventually plant.\n\n**(D) Correct.** The company took the incentive and still reduced total forest, which works against the law's goal.\n\n**(E) Too Strong.** One company's swap doesn't support a massive decrease in mature forests.\n\n## PT124-S2-Q25 | Must Be True | B\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Most serious students are happy. Most serious students go to graduate school. All students who go to graduate school are overworked.\n\n**Evaluate:** Two \"most\" statements about the same group must overlap. More than half of serious students are happy and more than half go to graduate school, so some serious students are both. Those graduate students are overworked. So some happy students are overworked.\n\n**Goal:** Some happy students are overworked.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Unsupported.** We know some overworked students are happy, not most. Plenty of overworked students may not be serious or happy.\n\n**(B) Correct.** Two \"mosts\" overlap, so some serious students are happy and in graduate school. Graduate students are overworked.\n\n**(C) Reversed.** Some serious students are overworked. This says every overworked student is serious.\n\n**(D) Unsupported.** The overlap could be complete: every serious graduate student could be happy.\n\n**(E) Too Strong.** Only most serious students go to graduate school. The rest might not be overworked.\n\n## PT139-S1-Q10 | Must Be True | D\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Large nahcolite deposits formed in salty lakes during the Eocene. In salty water, nahcolite can form only when carbon dioxide is at least 1,125 parts per million.\n\n**Evaluate:** Nahcolite forming in salty water → carbon dioxide at least 1,125 ppm. It did form, so carbon dioxide reached that level at least while those deposits formed. That's only part of the Eocene, and says nothing about other times.\n\n**Goal:** Carbon dioxide was at least 1,125 ppm during some part of the Eocene.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Unsupported.** We know nothing about carbon dioxide after the Eocene.\n\n**(B) Unsupported.** We know carbon dioxide was high at some point. Nothing says it swung up and down.\n\n**(C) Reversed.** Carbon dioxide is required for nahcolite in salty water. Nothing says high carbon dioxide made lakes salty.\n\n**(D) Correct.** Nahcolite formed, so its requirement was met during at least part of the Eocene.\n\n**(E) Unsupported.** Nahcolite could have formed since then whenever carbon dioxide was high enough.\n\n## PT139-S4-Q2 | Must Be True | D\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Acrylics provide everything a good paint should provide. Even acrylics can't correct defects like badly cracked paint. Those defects point to an underlying problem that needs repair.\n\n**Evaluate:** Put the first two statements together. Acrylics give everything a good paint should. Acrylics can't fix cracked paint. So fixing cracked paint is not something a good paint must do.\n\n**Goal:** Correcting surface defects is not a requirement of house paint.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Unsupported.** Water damage is one example of an underlying cause. Harsh weather could be another.\n\n**(B) Too Strong.** Acrylics provide everything a good paint should, but other paints might too.\n\n**(C) Unsupported.** Painting over other paint types never comes up.\n\n**(D) Correct.** Acrylics meet every requirement of a good paint and still can't fix cracks. So fixing cracks isn't a requirement.\n\n**(E) Unsupported.** Color range never comes up.\n\n## PT144-S4-Q1 | Sufficient Assumption | C\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Vadim is going to be laid off.\n\n**Evidence:** Management has decided to lay off a programmer. The firm always lays off the most recently hired programmer.\n\n**Evaluate:** The policy picks the most recently hired programmer. Nothing yet says that's Vadim. Connect Vadim to the policy and the conclusion follows.\n\n**Goal:** Vadim is the most recently hired programmer.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Irrelevant.** What the firm values doesn't change the strict layoff policy, and still doesn't name Vadim.\n\n**(B) Irrelevant.** Whether the policy was explained to Vadim doesn't make Vadim the one laid off.\n\n**(C) Correct.** The firm lays off the most recent hire. If that's Vadim, Vadim is laid off.\n\n**(D) Irrelevant.** The policy is based on hiring order, not work quality.\n\n**(E) Irrelevant.** Whether the policy is good doesn't change whom it selects.\n\n## PT145-S4-Q24 | Sufficient Assumption | D\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Unless the critics are mistaken, Mallotech is not accurately portraying itself as socially responsible.\n\n**Evidence:** Critics say many Mallotech employees work in unsanitary conditions.\n\n**Evaluate:** If the critics are right, there are unsanitary conditions. The conclusion says that means Mallotech isn't socially responsible. The missing link is unsanitary conditions → not socially responsible.\n\n**Goal:** A socially responsible company would not have employees in unsanitary conditions.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Irrelevant.** This is about lying, but the argument is about the working conditions themselves. Mallotech could be truthful about the conditions and still not be socially responsible.\n\n**(B) Irrelevant.** Nothing says Mallotech is concealing anything.\n\n**(C) Irrelevant.** This only confirms the critics. It doesn't connect unsanitary conditions to social responsibility.\n\n**(D) Correct.** If the critics are right, Mallotech has unsanitary conditions, so it isn't socially responsible, so its portrayal is inaccurate.\n\n**(E) Irrelevant.** Management quality never comes up.\n\n## PT156-S2-Q18 | Sufficient Assumption | C\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** The city council's objective is not to preserve the quality and availability of local rentals.\n\n**Evidence:** The council passed rent control. A study shows rent control lowers quality and availability.\n\n**Evaluate:** A study showing rent control hurts rentals doesn't tell us what the council wanted. Maybe it never saw the study or disagreed with it. If the council members who voted for rent control agreed it hurts rentals, then voting for it means they didn't aim to preserve them.\n\n**Goal:** The council members who voted for rent control agree with the study.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Irrelevant.** An impartial study makes the facts stronger, but says nothing about what the council believed or intended.\n\n**(B) Irrelevant.** Whether the council should consider rent control doesn't reveal its objective.\n\n**(C) Correct.** If they knew rent control hurts rentals and passed it anyway, preserving rentals wasn't their goal.\n\n**(D) Irrelevant.** Some members profiting doesn't show the council as a whole didn't care about rentals.\n\n**(E) Irrelevant.** Acting arbitrarily sometimes doesn't tell us what the objective was here.\n\n## PT156-S2-Q25 | Sufficient Assumption | B\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Under Newtonian theory, you don't need a theory of what the Sun and planets are made of to calculate their orbits.\n\n**Evidence:** Under Newtonian theory, gravitational force depends only on mass and distance, not on what bodies are made of.\n\n**Evaluate:** The evidence is about gravitational force. The conclusion is about orbits. Bridge them: if calculating orbits requires only gravitational force, and gravitational force doesn't depend on composition, then orbits don't need composition either.\n\n**Goal:** Under Newtonian theory, calculating orbits requires only gravitational forces.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Irrelevant.** This reverses the relationship and still says nothing about orbits.\n\n**(B) Correct.** Orbits need only gravitational force, and gravitational force ignores composition. So orbits don't need composition.\n\n**(C) Opposite.** If the theory is mistaken, it undercuts the argument rather than completing it.\n\n**(D) Irrelevant.** Composition being enough to find mass doesn't show it's unnecessary for orbits.\n\n**(E) Irrelevant.** This links force to distance but doesn't say orbits depend only on force.\n\n## PT156-S4-Q7 | Must Be True | A\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** In a truly visual art form, like painting, time plays no essential role. Temporal art forms require performance, which means a fixed order and a roughly fixed amount of time. Poetry looks visual but must be performed.\n\n**Evaluate:** Performance → fixed order and time → time plays an essential role. Truly visual art has no essential role for time. Take the contrapositive: truly visual art doesn't essentially involve performance.\n\n**Goal:** Truly visual art forms don't essentially involve performance.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** Performance requires fixed time, and visual art has no essential role for time. So visual art doesn't require performance.\n\n**(B) Opposite.** Poetry is temporal and performed, like music, not visual like painting.\n\n**(C) Unsupported.** Spatiality never comes up, and nothing says the two can't coexist.\n\n**(D) Unsupported.** Temporal art needs a fixed order and time. A painting might need long study with no fixed order at all.\n\n**(E) Too Strong.** Poetry and music are examples of temporal art. Nothing says they are the only performed arts.\n\n## PT156-S4-Q22 | Sufficient Assumption | E\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** An effective acting performance doesn't call attention to the fact that it's a performance.\n\n**Evidence:** Calling attention to the performance makes it harder for the audience to empathize with the character. Effective performances don't detract from the audience's appreciation of a play.\n\n**Evaluate:** Chain it. Calls attention → harder to empathize. Effective → doesn't detract. The gap: harder to empathize → detracts. With that link: calls attention → harder to empathize → detracts → not effective.\n\n**Goal:** Making empathy harder detracts from appreciation of the play.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Irrelevant.** This is about what a play needs, not what makes a single performance ineffective.\n\n**(B) Reversed.** Not calling attention → not detracting. We need calling attention → detracting.\n\n**(C) Irrelevant.** Enhancing appreciation never connects to calling attention.\n\n**(D) Irrelevant.** Enhancing appreciation isn't the same as not detracting, and nothing links it to calling attention.\n\n**(E) Correct.** Calling attention makes empathy harder, which detracts from appreciation, which an effective performance never does.\n\n## PT156-S4-Q23 | Flaw | A\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** If Logichut has no creative employees, its management must be open to new ideas.\n\n**Evidence:** The software industry is growing rapidly. Rapid company growth → innovation → creative employees or open management. Logichut is a software company.\n\n**Evaluate:** The rule applies to a company growing rapidly. The industry is growing, but that doesn't mean every company in it is. The argument moves from a property of the whole industry to Logichut. That's a whole-to-part flaw.\n\n**Goal:** The argument assumes each company in a growing industry is itself growing.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** The industry is growing, so the argument treats Logichut as growing. A whole's property doesn't pass to each part.\n\n**(B) Not the flaw.** The argument uses innovation correctly as requiring creative employees or open management.\n\n**(C) Not the flaw.** \"Said to have\" is only a premise for the \"if so\" conditional. The argument doesn't conclude it's true.\n\n**(D) Not the flaw.** Growth is used correctly as requiring innovation. The problem is assuming Logichut grows at all.\n\n**(E) Not the flaw.** The argument allows both. It only says management must be open if there are no creative employees.\n\n## PT159-S1-Q18 | Must Be True | A\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Tapping a healthy maple with a trunk 12 inches or wider will not harm it. Several kinds of maple can be tapped. Sugar maples are best for syrup.\n\n**Evaluate:** Healthy and 12+ inches → tapping won't harm. Take the contrapositive: if tapping harms a tree, it's not healthy or it's under 12 inches. If a tree is over 12 inches and tapping harms it, it must be unhealthy.\n\n**Goal:** A tree over 12 inches that is harmed by tapping is unhealthy.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** Harmed by tapping means not healthy or under 12 inches. It's over 12 inches, so it's unhealthy.\n\n**(B) Unsupported.** Health and trunk size are never linked.\n\n**(C) Unsupported.** Sap production of harmed trees never comes up.\n\n**(D) Negated.** Healthy and large → no harm. def parse_drafts():
    slots = {}
    for path in DRAFTS:
        text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        for sec in text.split("\n## ")[1:]:
            head = sec.split("\n", 1)[0]
            slot, qtype, key = [x.strip() for x in head.split("|")]
            steps, notes = [], {}
            bd = sec.split("### Argument Breakdown", 1)
            if len(bd) == 2:
                part = bd[1].split("### Choice Notes", 1)[0]
                for m in re.finditer(r"^\*\*(.+?):\*\* (.+?)(?=\n\n\*\*|\Z)", part.strip(), re.S | re.M):
                    steps.append((m.group(1).strip(), m.group(2).strip()))
            cn = sec.split("### Choice Notes", 1)[1] if "### Choice Notes" in sec else ""
            for m in re.finditer(r"^\*\*\(([A-E])\) (.+?)\.\*\* (.+?)(?=\n\n\*\*\(|\Z)", cn.strip(), re.S | re.M):
                notes[m.group(1)] = (m.group(2).strip(), m.group(3).strip())
            slots[slot] = dict(type=qtype, key=key, steps=steps, notes=notes)
    return slots


def main():
    drafts = parse_drafts()
    bank = {}
    for f in BANK.glob("PT*-S*-LR.json"):
        for b in json.loads(f.read_text(encoding="utf-8")):
            bank[f"{b['practiceTest']}-S{b['sectionNumber']}-Q{b['questionNumber']}"] = b
    qs = {q["qid"]: q for q in records("lr_questions")}
    exq = defaultdict(list)
    for e in records("lr_explanations"):
        if e["style"] in ("single", "standard"):
            exq[e["question_id"]].append(e)
    st = defaultdict(list)
    for s in records("lr_explanation_steps"):
        st[s["explanation_id"]].append(s)
    nt = defaultdict(dict)
    for n in records("lr_explanation_choice_notes"):

### 2. What the best ones do

- **Decide recipe or slogan first, and say why.** Conditional, quantifier and repeated terms mean diagram; one premise or no formal language means state the moral (PT146-S1-Q23 declines to diagram despite "only" and "never"; PT108-S2-Q16 gives both).
- **Write the prediction as a numbered ingredient list: number of premises, claim type (conditional, most, some, fact), conclusion type and strength** (PT151-S2-Q19, PT144-S4-Q22). Then name which ingredients are essential and which are only filters (PT151-S2-Q19 on the AND outcome).
- **Cut on the conclusion first, by type and strength.** "Can't avoid" vs. "can't rule out" (PT151-S2-Q19 D); "never" and "cannot" vs. "unlikely" (PT150-S3-Q23 A, C); possible or certain vs. probable (PT112-S4-Q9 A, E).
- **Run one test on every choice and write out what a matching answer would have said.** PT149-S3-Q23 writes the proper conclusion for each choice before showing the actual one; PT106-S3-Q26 rewrites trap A into its matching form.
- **Put the original and the choice side by side.** Tables (PT149-S1-Q25) or a running tally of wrong moves (PT152-S1-Q23: denies trigger, confirms trigger, confirms outcome) make the break visible without prose.
- **Give the popular trap the longest note and say what it gets right before what breaks.** PT111-S4-Q23 A (34%, within one person vs. across people); PT117-S3-Q16 D (22%); PT152-S2-Q19 C (28%, Mars example).
- **Say out loud when the key is imperfect and which mismatch doesn't matter.** PT117-S3-Q16 (some vs. many is logically irrelevant); PT106-S3-Q26 (weak conclusion match, best gist); PT150-S3-Q23 (three premises packed into one).
- **Teach the translation rule the question depends on.** "Unless" into the trigger (PT112-S4-Q9); negative to positive quantifiers (PT152-S2-Q19); a recommendation is an implicit comparison (PT117-S4-Q21).
- **Flag surface bait as a signal.** Same topic or copied wording is usually the trap: PT102-S2-Q22 C and D (government subsidy topic), PT151-S2-Q19 A ("the only conclusion one can draw").

### 3. What the weaker candidates got wrong

- **Flattened diagrams that no longer read.** PT108-S3-Q24, PT120-S4-Q25, PT134-S3-Q25 and PT140-S3-Q24 lost their line breaks, so the recipe (the whole point on formal Parallel) is unreadable.
- **Verdict-by-template on the popular trap.** PT151-S4-Q25 gives D (16%) the same pasted "does the conclusion match the trigger" block as A and C; PT103-S1-Q24 dismisses D (17%) in one line.
- **Eliminating on a distinction the test does not make.** PT140-S2-Q17 eliminates A and E because "confident" is weaker than "sure".
- **Tone at the key's expense.** PT110-S3-Q25 calls the correct answer "kind of terrible" and leans on outside knowledge to reconstruct Terry's point.
- **Checklist notes with no reason.** PT148-S3-Q26 C lists the claim inventory and stops; PT140-S3-Q24 C to E are yes/no lines.

395	  STEP Original Argument | Premise: People who have never been pushed beyond their comfort zone never do all they can. (Never pushed → never doing all they can.)
396	Premise: Alex has not done all he is capable of doing.
397	Conclusion: Alex has never been pushed beyond his comfort zone.
398	  STEP Evaluate | The flaw is affirming the consequent / mistaking necessary for sufficient. The first premise gives: never pushed → not doing all you can. The argument observes that Alex is not doing all he can and concludes he was never pushed. But "not doing all you can" can have causes other than "never pushed" — laziness, illness, bad luck. The condition (never pushed) is sufficient for "not doing all you can," but the argument treats it as if it were necessary.
399	  STEP Goal | Find an answer with the same flaw: a conditional ("X → Y"), then observation that Y holds, then conclusion that X holds — affirming the consequent.
400	  STEP Argument Form | Never pushed → not doing all you can. Alex is not doing all he can. Therefore Alex was never pushed.
401	  STEP Goal | Find an answer that takes a conditional, observes the consequent (Y) holds, and concludes the antecedent (X) holds — the same affirming-the-consequent flaw.
402	  STEP The Original | The argument says: "People never pushed always fail to do all they can. Alex is failing to do all he can, so Alex must never have been pushed."
403	  STEP Evaluate | This is "affirming the consequent" — a classic logic mistake. The premise gives one cause of underperformance (never being pushed). The argument then sees underperformance and assumes that one cause must be at work. But underperformance can come from many sources: laziness, illness, lack of resources. Just because everyone never-pushed underperforms does not mean every underperformer was never pushed.
404	It is like saying: "Everyone who has the flu has a cough. Bob has a cough. So Bob has the flu." Bob could have a cold or allergies. Coughing does not narrow it down.
405	  STEP Goal | Find the answer with this exact form: a conditional, an observation that the conclusion side of the conditional holds, then a conclusion that the original cause holds.
406	  NOTE A | This is the parallel flaw. Map it onto the original:
407	
408	**Original:** Never-pushed → underperforming. Alex is underperforming. So Alex was never pushed.
409	
410	**This answer:** Has a dog → knows companionship. Alicia knows companionship. So Alicia has a dog.
411	
412	Same form, same mistake. Knowing companionship has many possible sources (friends, family, cats), just as underperformance has many sources. Picking just one cause because the result happened is the flaw — affirming the consequent — and this answer commits it identically.
413	  NOTE B | Map this one out: discoverer → examined all solutions. Fran is not a discoverer (denying antecedent). Conclusion: Fran has not explored all solutions (denying consequent). This is a different mistake from the original. The original moves from observed effect to assumed cause; this one moves from "no cause" to "no effect." Wrong shape.
414	  NOTE C | This argument is actually valid. "Not challenged → not accomplishing all" — and Jill accomplishes all. By contrapositive, she must be challenged. That is solid reasoning. We need a flawed parallel, not a valid one.
415	  NOTE D | This argument applies a definition correctly. "A polygon is X. This object is X. So this object is a polygon." That is not flawed — definitions work biconditionally (anything fitting the definition is a polygon, anything that is a polygon fits the definition). Valid reasoning, so not a parallel to the flawed original.
416	  NOTE E | This one gets messy — the conditional is about losing something irreplaceable, but Jon is described as lax with replaceable things, and the conclusion is he never lost *anything*. The scope keeps shifting in ways the original does not. The structure does not cleanly mirror the original's "premise → consequent observed → antecedent concluded" pattern.

538	  D The nation's voters know that electing Gomez would be the best way to help the nation. The ten voters we polled all agreed that the policies Gomez is committed to would help the nation more than any other policies.
539	  E We know that electing Gomez would be the best course for the nation to follow because, of ten voters we surveyed, each agreed that electing Gomez would help the nation.
540	===== PT139-S4-Q10 Parallel Reasoning KEY B
541	In a test of fuel efficiency, car X and car Y yielded the same average fuel mileage, even though car X was driven in a less fuel-efficient manner than car Y was. Thus, car X is more fuel efficient than car Y.
542	Q: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
543	  A In an experiment, subject X consistently gave lower pain ratings in response to pinpricks than subject Y did. Therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that subjects X and Y experience pain differently.
544	  B Our hamster gained the same amount of weight as our neighbors' hamster, even though our hamster ate more than theirs. So it must be that our hamster burned more calories than theirs did.
545	  C When on his bicycle, Roland makes better time coasting down a hill than pedaling on a horizontal path. So he would make even better time on the hills if he were to pedal rather than coast.
546	  D When asked to judge the value of various pieces of antique furniture, I gave lower estimates on average than you did. So in those cases where we both gave the same estimate, I must have overestimated the piece's value.
547	  E Jean demonstrates a high level of visual acuity when she wears prescription glasses. Thus, it must be that without those prescription glasses, she would demonstrate a lower level of visual acuity.
548	===== PT159-S1-Q23 Parallel Reasoning KEY A
549	During last year’s flu season no one who was vaccinated contracted the flu. This year every student at South High School has been vaccinated. So this flu season none of the students at South High School will contract the flu.
550	Q: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
551	  A No camper who used insect repellent last month was disturbed by mosquitoes. Since everyone in our campsite has applied insect repellent tonight, none of us will be disturbed by mosquitoes tonight.
552	  B Last year, Marie purchased a car that had been well maintained. Since Marie will certainly continue to maintain the car this year, the car is unlikely to have mechanical problems this year.
553	  C Last year, no student with perfect attendance failed a class, and all students in advanced history had perfect attendance. So no student in advanced history last year failed the class.
554	  D All the fruit we purchased yesterday was fresh. All the fruit we bought yesterday is in the refrigerator. Therefore, all the fruit in the refrigerator is fresh.
555	  E No sparrow eats seeds with hard shells. All seeds of this tree have hard shells. So no sparrow will eat the seeds of this tree.
556	===== PT159-S1-Q25 Parallel Flaw KEY D
557	Artist: I have never won a prize at the Art Competition, even though several of my submitted paintings have received widespread recognition and have sold thousands of copies as posters. I know six other popular artists who have submitted works to that competition and fared no better. Thus, winning the Art Competition proves that an artist is no good.
558	Q: The pattern of flawed reasoning in which one of the following arguments most closely resembles that in the artist’s argument?
559	  A Researcher: I have never won a prize at the Science Competition, although I have obtained patents for several of my inventions and they have been extremely lucrative. Other scientists have had similar experiences. Therefore, the judges are using some criterion other than marketability to judge the inventions.
560	  B Cook: I always win a prize at the Cooking Competition, even though my entries are regarded by the general public as unusual and unappealing. Other cooks have reported similar experiences. Thus, winning proves that one’s culinary creation is not to most people’s taste.
561	  C Professor: The same essays that have won nothing in some years at the Philosophical Essay Competition have won the grand prize in other years. So the essays are not judged entirely on quality.
562	  D Student: The student government never takes my proposals seriously, even when these proposals have the support of most students. Others have also introduced widely supported proposals, but the student government has not seriously considered theirs either. So the student government takes only bad proposals seriously.
563	  E Travel agent: When I do my most creative and dedicated work, the airlines reduce my commissions. And when I do rushed work, they send me fruit baskets in gratitude. I conclude that airlines want to discourage good ideas and hard work.
564	===== PT159-S3-Q10 Parallel Flaw KEY B
565	For years, Glenville had the highest apartment rents in the metropolitan region in which it is located. This year, Glenville has only the third highest apartment rents in the region. Therefore, it must cost less to rent an apartment in Glenville now than it used to.
566	Q: Which one of the following arguments demonstrates most effectively by parallel reasoning that the argument above is flawed?
567	  A Because Brenda’s kitten’s veterinary bills are lower than her puppy’s veterinary bills, the kitten must be healthier than the puppy.
568	  B Because Brenda’s kitten was larger than her puppy a while ago but is now smaller than the puppy, the kitten must have shrunk.
569	  C Because Brenda’s kitten was born a week before her puppy was, Brenda must have gotten the kitten first.
570	  D Because Brenda’s kitten eats less than her puppy does, the kitten is unlikely to become overweight.

{"file_path": "C:\\Users\\Joshu\\dev\\ai-os\\corpus\\lr-explanations\\drafts\\batch-12-flaw-part-a.md", "content": "---\ntype: draft\nsubject: LR batch 12, part A, 26 slots (Parallel Flaw, every label spelling)\nstatus: draft\ncreated: 2026-10-02\n---\n\n# Batch 12, part A: Parallel Flaw\n\nEvery gap labelled \"Parallel Flaw\" or \"Parallel flawed method of reasoning\". Twenty-two are in the database with no explanation, one needs notes only, and three are not in the database.\n\nModelled on `models/Parallel.md`: name the flaw in one line, then check each choice for the same move. Cut on the conclusion first, and give the popular trap the longest note.\n\nLabels: Conclusion / Evidence / Evaluate / Goal.\n\n## PT101-S3-Q16 | Parallel Flaw | A\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** The accusation that K falsified data should be dismissed.\n\n**Evidence:** The data in question are gone. K's more recent data were checked and none were falsified.\n\n**Evaluate:** The accusation is about the missing data. The evidence is about different, later data. Clean later work doesn't show the earlier work was clean. The flaw: dismiss a charge about one set of records using other records.\n\n**Goal:** Find an argument that dismisses a charge about lost records using evidence from different records.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** The records that matter were destroyed, so L's current clients' clean records are used to dismiss the charge. Same move.\n\n**(B) Bad Conclusion Match.** This concludes the charge should be discussed, not dismissed, and the evidence actually supports the charge.\n\n**(C) Bad Premise Match.** The other work came after N's, so N couldn't have copied it. That is a real defense based on the evidence at issue.\n\n**(D) Bad Conclusion Match.** This supports the accusation instead of dismissing it.\n\n**(E) Bad Premise Match.** This relies on disagreement about the public interest, not on evidence from unrelated records.\n\n## PT101-S3-Q21 | Parallel Flaw | A\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Millville used more electricity this August than last August.\n\n**Evidence:** Each day's electricity use is directly proportional to that day's peak humidity. Average peak humidity was higher this August.\n\n**Evaluate:** Recipe: a quantity in each unit is proportional to a factor in that unit. The factor averaged higher this period than last. So the total quantity was higher this period. Look for the same pieces: per-unit proportion, comparison of the factor across two periods, conclusion about the total.\n\n**Goal:** Per-unit proportion, factor higher overall this period, so the total is higher this period.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** Supplies in each class are proportional to that class's students. More students overall last year, so more supplies last year. Every piece lines up.\n\n**(B) Bad Conclusion Match.** This compares painting courses with sculpture courses, not one quantity across two periods.\n\n**(C) Bad Conclusion Match.** This ends in a recommendation about what the institute must do, not a comparison of totals.\n\n**(D) Bad Premise Match.** Fees are proportional to the number of classes per student, but the evidence is about the number of students. The factor in the evidence isn't the one in the proportion.\n\n**(E) Bad Conclusion Match.** This links two proportions to a third. It never compares two periods.\n\n## PT102-S4-Q12 | Parallel Flaw | D\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** The teaching has improved.\n\n**Evidence:** The principal believes bad teaching causes failures. Failures disappeared.\n\n**Evaluate:** Nothing was observed about the teaching. The principal assumes the theory is right, sees the effect go away, and concludes the cause went away. Failures could have stopped for many other reasons.\n\n**Goal:** Find someone who holds a theory about a cause, sees the effect stop, and concludes the cause stopped.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Premise Match.** Here the cause (overeating) is observed to stop and the effect is predicted. The original observes the effect and infers the cause.\n\n**(B) Bad Premise Match.** The manager actually changed the jobs. In the original, nobody did anything to the teaching.\n\n**(C) Bad Premise Match.** The nutritionist hands out charts and concludes the complaints stopped. No cause is inferred from a vanished effect.\n\n**(D) Correct.** The manager's theory: complaints come from too little work. Complaints stopped, so the manager concludes the workers are busy. Same move.\n\n**(E) Bad Premise Match.** This relies on a report that the cause stopped and then concludes the effect stopped. That runs the other way.\n\n## PT105-S1-Q22 | Parallel Flaw | B\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Supporters of a bicycle helmet law are misguided.\n\n**Evidence:** Walking and drunk driving cause far more deaths, yet nobody calls for banning walking or alcohol.\n\n**Evaluate:** The editorial rejects a safety measure for one risk because bigger risks elsewhere aren't banned. But the comparison is to banning whole activities, not to a modest safety rule. A bigger risk going unaddressed doesn't make the smaller rule foolish.\n\n**Goal:** Find an argument that rejects a safety rule because bigger risks elsewhere aren't met with bans.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Premise Match.** This says pilots will likely die of something else first. It doesn't point to bigger risks that go unbanned.\n\n**(B) Correct.** Goggles for lab workers are called foolish because more people get sick from food and disease, and nobody suggests banning eating or socializing. Same move.\n\n**(C) Bad Premise Match.** This argues about the right order of learning. No risk comparison.\n\n**(D) Bad Premise Match.** This is about timing and cost. A reasonable objection, not the original's flaw.\n\n**(E) Bad Premise Match.** This narrows the rule to those at risk. It doesn't reject a rule by pointing to bigger unbanned risks.\n\n## PT105-S4-Q23 | Parallel Flaw | D\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Donna's claim must be false.\n\n**Evidence:** Donna says she found the Benin exhibition less interesting than others. All the critics say it is the most interesting in years.\n\n**Evaluate:** Donna is reporting her own reaction. The critics' opinion can't show she didn't have that reaction. The flaw: using others' judgment to refute someone's report of personal taste.\n\n**Goal:** Find an argument that refutes a claim about personal taste with what others think.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Premise Match.** Whether a task is finished is a fact, not a matter of taste. The supervisor's word is relevant evidence.\n\n**(B) Bad Premise Match.** Morris was out of the country. That is factual evidence, and it does show the claim false.\n\n**(C) Bad Premise Match.** This pits two people's reports about motives against each other. No outside consensus about taste.\n\n**(D) Correct.** Loren says the fish tastes good. Food experts say it's dreadful, so the argument calls Loren's claim false. Same move.\n\n**(E) Bad Premise Match.** The atlas gives a fact about mountain heights. That does refute Douglas's claim.\n\n## PT106-S3-Q21 | Parallel Flaw | D\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** The city has no obligation to provide trash cans.\n\n**Evidence:** If the law punishes littering, the city must provide trash cans. The law doesn't punish littering.\n\n**Evaluate:** Punishes littering → obligation. The argument denies the trigger and concludes the result is absent. That's denying the antecedent: the obligation could come from somewhere else.\n\n**Goal:** If A then B. Not A. So not B.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Premise Match.** Holiday → bakery closed. Closed, so holiday. That affirms the result to conclude the trigger, a different flaw.\n\n**(B) Bad Premise Match.** This reads as a contrapositive: no balloons yet, so not the party. Different shape.\n\n**(C) Bad Premise Match.** Success requires adherence. Adherence, so success. That treats a requirement as a guarantee, a different flaw.\n\n**(D) Correct.** Late flight → miss meeting. Not late, so won't miss. Same denial of the trigger.\n\n**(E) Bad Premise Match.** Enforced → some jailed. No one jailed, so not enforced. That is a valid contrapositive.\n\n## PT107-S1-Q23 | Parallel Flaw | B\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Some people who appreciate poetry are illogical.\n\n**Evidence:** No scientist appreciates poetry. Most scientists are logical.\n\n**Evaluate:** Recipe: No A are B. Most A are C. So some B are not C. The facts about scientists say nothing about the people who appreciate poetry, since none of them are scientists. The conclusion jumps to a new group.\n\n**Goal:** No A are B, most A are C, so some B are not C.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Conclusion Match.** No marsupials lay eggs, most are Australian, so some Australians don't lay eggs. That's valid: the marsupials themselves are those Australians. The original's conclusion is about the excluded group.\n\n**(B) Correct.** No fathers want candy at bedtime. Most fathers are adults. So some candy-wanters are not adults. Same recipe, same flaw.\n\n**(C) Bad Conclusion Match.** This concludes California wine is inferior. That's a claim about the \"most\" group, not about the excluded group.\n\n**(D) Bad Conclusion Match.** Valid: most instant film is color, and no color film is that sharp, so some instant film isn't.\n\n**(E) Bad Conclusion Match.** This says some tax-likers are honest. The original concludes the excluded group lacks the \"most\" trait, so a match would say some are dishonest.\n\n## PT108-S3-Q14 | Parallel Flaw | A\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Miller: Jurgens should be elected.\n\n**Evidence:** Wu says Jurgens is dishonest. Miller replies that honest people usually aren't tough enough to run a city.\n\n**Evaluate:** Miller doesn't defend Jurgens's dishonesty. Miller attacks the opposite trait, honesty, by naming a downside. Showing honesty has a cost doesn't show Jurgens is a good choice, or even tough.\n\n**Goal:** Wu objects to a trait; the reply names a downside of the opposite trait.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** Wu objects to slow service. Miller says fast service often means poor food. Same move: attack the opposite trait.\n\n**(B) Bad Premise Match.** This is the popular trap. Wu objects to aggression, and Miller praises aggression itself (\"aggressive people don't get pushed around\"). That defends the criticized trait directly. The original attacks the opposite trait instead.\n\n**(C) Bad Premise Match.** Miller praises brightness itself, the trait Wu criticized.\n\n**(D) Bad Premise Match.** Miller defends the high price itself as a sign of quality.\n\n**(E) Bad Conclusion Match.** Miller recommends a different applicant. The original argues for the same candidate Wu rejected.\n\n## PT109-S1-Q15 | Parallel Flaw | C\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Mary would make a good Drackedary player.\n\n**Evidence:** Good Drackedary players are skilled with their hands. Mary is a skilled watchmaker.\n\n**Evaluate:** Good player → skilled hands. Mary has skilled hands, so the argument concludes she's a good player. That reverses the rule: skilled hands are required, not enough.\n\n**Goal:** All A are B. X shows B. So X is A.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Premise Match.** Long legs → good runner, and Daryl's family has long legs. That applies the rule in the right direction.\n\n**(B) Bad Premise Match.** Writers → enjoy reading. Julie writes, so Julie enjoys reading. That's valid.\n\n**(C) Correct.** Race drivers → good reflexes. Chris has good reflexes from table tennis, so the argument concludes Chris would be a good driver. Same reversal.\n\n**(D) Bad Premise Match.** \"Often played by an actor\" is a \"many\" claim. Concluding Erwin \"must\" be an actor overstates a generalization, a different flaw.\n\n**(E) Bad Conclusion Match.** Learning \"eventually\" turns into \"in a day or two.\" That's an exaggerated timeline, not a reversal.\n\n## PT109-S3-Q18 | Parallel Flaw | B\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Industrial activities are purely beneficial to agriculture.\n\n**Evidence:** More carbon dioxide intensifies photosynthesis, and industry raises carbon dioxide.\n\n**Evaluate:** One benefit is shown. The conclusion says the activity is purely beneficial, ignoring every possible harm.\n\n**Goal:** One benefit shown, so the thing is entirely good.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Conclusion Match.** This argues more is always better. The original goes from one benefit to no harm at all.\n\n**(B) Correct.** Exercise prevents some ills, so the argument concludes no harm can come from it. Same jump.\n\n**(C) Bad Conclusion Match.** This recommends fasting from a weight-gain fact. No \"purely good\" claim.\n\n**(D) Bad Conclusion Match.** A comparison leads to abandoning one option entirely. That's a different overreach.\n\n**(E) Bad Conclusion Match.** This goes from one harm to avoiding the drug. Opposite direction from the original.\n\n## PT109-S3-Q22 | Parallel | C\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** If relativity is correct, either the tachyon prediction is wrong or tachyons travel backward in time.\n\n**Evidence:** Relativity says nothing can travel forward in time faster than light. Quantum mechanics predicts tachyons travel faster than light.\n\n**Evaluate:** A trusted theory rules something out. A source says it happened. So if the theory holds, either the source is wrong or the case escapes the rule's condition (\"forward in time\").\n\n**Goal:** Theory forbids X; a report says X; so if the theory holds, the report is wrong or the case falls outside the rule.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Conclusion Match.** This prefers one origin theory over another. No conditional conclusion with two options.\n\n**(B) Bad Conclusion Match.** This concludes the defendant is guilty, a flat verdict.\n\n**(C) Correct.** The brain can't survive long without oxygen. A witness says the shaman survived a week buried. So if medicine is right, the witness is wrong or the brain didn't lack oxygen. Same structure.\n\n**(D) Bad Conclusion Match.** This weighs evidence between two burial sites.\n\n**(E) Bad Conclusion Match.** This draws a prediction from a theory. No conflict between a theory and a report.\n\n## PT109-S4-Q6 | Parallel Flaw | C\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** The worker won't trim one tree's branches.\n\n**Evidence:** The owners have said they might cut the tree down.\n\n**Evaluate:** \"Might\" isn't \"will.\" If the tree stays, the lines are at risk. The worker skips needed preventive work based on a possibility.\n\n**Goal:** Skip needed maintenance because the item might be removed.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Premise Match.** Inspecting the most-used wells first under a time limit is sensible prioritization.\n\n**(B) Bad Premise Match.** Choosing cheaper pipe to save money is a cost tradeoff, not skipping needed work.\n\n**(C) Correct.** The van is only \"tentatively scheduled\" to be junked, yet the mechanic skips its brakes. Same move.\n\n**(D) Bad Premise Match.** The candidate avoids areas where campaigning would actually backfire. That's a reason, not a possibility.\n\n**(E) Bad Premise Match.** Punishing everyone to catch one child is a different flaw.\n\n## PT110-S3-Q23 | Parallel Flaw | D\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Nonindustrial societies tend to be socially unified.\n\n**Evidence:** Societies that measure value mainly in money fragment. Nonindustrial societies don't measure value mainly in money.\n\n**Evaluate:** Money-measure → fragment. Not money-measure, so the argument concludes the opposite: unified. That denies the trigger and then claims the reverse result.\n\n**Goal:** A → B. Not A. So the opposite of B.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Premise Match.** This correctly says the rule doesn't apply to jackals and wolves. It's valid.\n\n**(B) Bad Premise Match.** This applies a \"usually\" rule to two specific places. A different flaw.\n\n**(C) Bad Premise Match.** This generalizes from insects to all arthropods, a part-to-whole flaw.\n\n**(D) Correct.** Poets often use nonliteral language. Journalists aren't poets, so the argument concludes they always speak literally. Same move: deny the trigger, claim the opposite.\n\n**(E) Bad Premise Match.** This applies the rule in its own direction: sophisticated machines cause trouble, computers are sophisticated. No denial of the trigger.\n\n## PT111-S4-Q6 | Parallel Flaw | B\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** No population control measures should be taken.\n\n**Evidence:** Population growth has been followed by equally strong economic growth.\n\n**Evaluate:** A concern is dismissed because the worrying thing happens alongside something good. The good result doesn't show the problem isn't real or that it caused the good.\n\n**Goal:** Dismiss a concern because it goes along with success, so take no action.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Premise Match.** This says subscribers should pay their share. No good result is used to dismiss a concern.\n\n**(B) Correct.** Complaints about the manager are dismissed because sales are rising, so no action is taken. Same move.\n\n**(C) Bad Conclusion Match.** This suggests a compromise. It doesn't dismiss the concern.\n\n**(D) Bad Premise Match.** This appeals to enjoyment and variety. No good outcome tied to the problem.\n\n**(E) Bad Premise Match.** This predicts prices will fall, a different reasoning error.\n\n## PT113-S4-Q4 | Parallel Flaw | E\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Greta Harris must be a high-earning CEO.\n\n**Evidence:** Most high-earning CEOs attended prestigious business schools. Greta attended one.\n\n**Evaluate:** Most A are B. X is B. So X is A. Most high earners went to these schools, but most graduates may not be high earners. The argument reverses the relationship.\n\n**Goal:** Most A are B; X is B; so X is A.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Premise Match.** Fred is already known to be high-strung. The leap is to future health problems.\n\n**(B) Bad Conclusion Match.** This compares two singers' future fame.\n\n**(C) Bad Conclusion Match.** This concludes something about Italians in general.\n\n**(D) Bad Conclusion Match.** This draws a causal conclusion about luck.\n\n**(E) Correct.** Most successful singers studied several languages. Eileen did, so the argument concludes she's a successful singer. Same reversal.\n\n## PT114-S1-Q16 | Parallel Flaw | D\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Officials shouldn't add police to fight rising crime.\n\n**Evidence:** More police is only a stopgap. It doesn't fix the root causes.\n\n**Evaluate:** A measure that only treats symptoms can still help. The argument rejects it just because it isn't a complete cure.\n\n**Goal:** Reject a remedy because it doesn't fix the root cause.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Premise Match.** The rules are said to make behavior worse. That's a real harm, not just failing to be a cure.\n\n**(B) Bad Premise Match.** Dams are said to worsen the biggest floods. Again, a harm.\n\n**(C) Bad Conclusion Match.** This recommends a cheaper option after weighing costs.\n\n**(D) Correct.** The drug only reduces the disease's worst effects instead of curing it, so the argument says stop prescribing it. Same move.\n\n**(E) Bad Conclusion Match.** This recommends looking for other approaches, not dropping a partial one.\n\n## PT114-S2-Q23 | Parallel Flaw | C\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Finalism is more plausible than people thought.\n\n**Evidence:** Finalism is universally rejected. A new book attacks it, but the book's arguments are confused.\n\n**Evaluate:** One bad argument against a view does nothing to support the view. The reviewer treats a failed attack as evidence for a widely rejected position.\n\n**Goal:** A rejected view; one attack on it fails; so the view is more plausible than believed.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Premise Match.** This refutes the evidence for the claim and then calls the claim likely true. That's the opposite of a failed attack.\n\n**(B) Bad Premise Match.** The view is already widely accepted, and the attackers are just inexperienced.\n\n**(C) Correct.** Engineers reject the claim that aluminum equals titanium. One engineer's argument against it is confused, so the claim \"makes more sense than engineers believe.\" Same move.\n\n**(D) Bad Conclusion Match.** This concludes an accepted view is false.\n\n**(E) Bad Premise Match.** The view is accepted by sociologists, not rejected, and the conclusion just reaffirms it.\n\n## PT115-S4-Q26 | Parallel Flaw | D\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Education quality will surely deteriorate.\n\n**Evidence:** Because of hiring freezes, quality won't improve.\n\n**Evaluate:** Not improving leaves two options: staying the same or getting worse. The argument ignores staying the same.\n\n**Goal:** Won't go up, so must go down.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Premise Match.** This picks one lunch from many, but it isn't about a direction of change with a middle option.\n\n**(B) Bad Premise Match.** This is a probability judgment about proof and disproof.\n\n**(C) Bad Conclusion Match.** \"It may become more discordant\" is a hedged conclusion, and a fair one. The original says \"surely,\" and that certainty is the flaw.\n\n**(D) Correct.** The temperature can't rise, so it must fall. That ignores staying the same, just like the original.\n\n**(E) Bad Premise Match.** A dead starter does mean the car won't start. Valid.\n\n## PT116-S2-Q24 | Parallel Flaw | C\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** The law shouldn't require seat belts in cars.\n\n**Evidence:** People may ride motorcycles without belts, and a motorcycle even with a belt is more dangerous than a car without one.\n\n**Evaluate:** A riskier activity is allowed without a safeguard, so the argument concludes a safer activity shouldn't require one. The two activities may be regulated for different reasons.\n\n**Goal:** A riskier activity is permitted unprotected, so a safer one shouldn't require protection.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Premise Match.** This argues snacks would improve nutrition. No riskier activity permitted.\n\n**(B) Bad Premise Match.** This compares productivity, not risk, and argues for allowing time off.\n\n**(C) Correct.** Standing at cliff edges is legal, and even sitting at a cliff edge is riskier than standing on a coaster. So the argument says parks should allow standing. Same move.\n\n**(D) Bad Conclusion Match.** This argues for a new restriction, the opposite direction.\n\n**(E) Bad Premise Match.** This compares two places that differ only in size. No risk comparison.\n\n## PT118-S3-Q21 | Parallel Flaw | A\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** The more statistics training, the better at experimental psychology research.\n\n**Evidence:** Experimental psychology requires statistics, and you can't understand those applications without training.\n\n**Evaluate:** The evidence says training is required. The conclusion says more training keeps making you better. A requirement doesn't mean more is always better.\n\n**Goal:** X is required for Y, so more X means more Y.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** People need love and support to avoid unhappiness, so the more love, the happier. Same jump from requirement to \"more is better.\"\n\n**(B) Bad Premise Match.** Annual raises do mean longer service brings more income. Reasonable.\n\n**(C) Bad Premise Match.** This is a causal claim about a condition building over time.\n\n**(D) Bad Conclusion Match.** This restates a requirement as a requirement. It never says more is better.\n\n**(E) Bad Premise Match.** This treats chemistry as nearly enough for medicine, a sufficiency flaw.\n\n## PT119-S4-Q20 | Parallel Flaw | D\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** We can make a car that is both fuel efficient and crash safe.\n\n**Evidence:** We can make a car twice as efficient. We can make a car that meets crash standards.\n\n**Evaluate:** Each feature is possible alone. That doesn't mean both are possible together. The features might conflict.\n\n**Goal:** A is possible and B is possible, so A and B together are possible.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Premise Match.** This uses a requirement to rule dishwashers out. Valid.\n\n**(B) Bad Conclusion Match.** This concludes a cause, not a combination.\n\n**(C) Bad Premise Match.** This combines two people's reports about facts. It's about testimony, not possibility.\n\n**(D) Correct.** A best-seller is possible, and a critics' favorite is possible, so the argument concludes one book can be both. Same move.\n\n**(E) Bad Premise Match.** This already says a combined machine is possible and concludes one will exist. A different flaw.\n\n## PT120-S4-Q17 | Parallel Flaw | A\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** Has a dog → knows companionship. Alicia knows companionship, so the argument concludes Alicia has a dog. Same reversal as the original: the result is observed and the trigger is assumed.\n\n**(B) Bad Premise Match.** Fran never discovered anything, so the argument concludes Fran never examined all solutions. 62	  STEP Goal | Find a question whose answer reveals whether the diet caused the high blood pressure or whether the rats already had it.
63	  STEP The Argument | Researchers fed rats a high-salt diet. A few months later, 75% of those rats had high blood pressure. The conclusion: salt is linked to high blood pressure in rats.
64	  STEP Evaluate | Notice what the argument is missing — a "before" picture. We only see the rats *after* the diet. What if 75% of them already had high blood pressure when the study began? Then the diet did not cause anything; we would just be observing what was already true.
65	It is like measuring the height of a group of basketball players, finding they are tall, and concluding that something they did made them tall. Maybe — but you would want to know how tall they were when you started.

72	Imagine the answer: "Most of the rats had high blood pressure before the study." Now the salt diet has not been shown to cause anything; the high blood pressure was already there.

74	Now imagine the opposite: "Almost none of the rats had high blood pressure before the study." Now the diet looks like it really did something — three-quarters of them developed high blood pressure during the study. The whole conclusion swings on this answer.

504	characters more automatically frees up mental resources for other activities.
